description: We are university students specializing in Data Science and AI Engineering, passionate about using data and AI to solve real-world challenges. This hackathon is an opportunity to combine our technical skills with real-world data, innovative ideas, and data-driven decision-making. We’re excited to build something meaningful, learn from others, and tackle a challenge with an international perspective.
summary: We built Abandoned but not Forgotten, an interactive website for children aged five to fourteen. A cartoon astronaut flies a rocket across the Solar System, from the Moon to the edge of interstellar space. At each of its eleven stops, the young explorer finds a machine that NASA sent there and left behind: the laser reflector Apollo 11 placed on the Moon, the Sojourner rover still resting on Mars, the DART spacecraft that changed an asteroid’s orbit, Voyager 1 drifting between the stars. Each machine opens into a 3D model that children can take apart, piece by piece, while the astronaut explains how it worked and what it taught us. The challenge asked us to tell the stories of spacecraft whose missions have ended. We answered by turning those stories into a journey, so that every quiet piece of hardware becomes a destination worth reaching. This matters because these machines carry decades of human curiosity, and a child who learns why they were sent may one day send the next one.
details:
What does your project do and how does it work?

The site takes children on a rocket journey through eleven stops, from Earth to Deep Space. At each one, an astronaut guide tells a short story and points to a machine NASA left there. Clicking it opens a 3D model children can take apart, a page explaining what it discovered, and its NASA sources. Each new world is reached by an animated flight, and progress is saved for next time.

What benefits does it have?

It turns hard science into something children want to explore. The language is simple, the child sets the pace, and every fact comes from NASA. It runs in any browser, with no installation or account.

What is the intended impact?

We want children to learn that space missions are built by people and remembered long after they go silent, and to leave curious enough to want to explore themselves.

What tools, coding languages, hardware and software did you use?

TypeScript, React and Vite for the website, GSAP for animation, and three.js for the 3D models. Python prepared the artwork, Vitest tested the code, and GitHub held it all. We also used an SI coding assistant (Claude), SI image generation assistants (Google Gemini, Manus , Nano Banana, ChatGPT), and an SI voice generation assistant (gpt 4o mini-tts). Everything was built on ordinary laptops.

How is your project creative?

Instead of a list of old spacecraft, it is a story with a guide and a route. Worlds unlock as children reach them, the machines can be pulled apart by hand, and every rocket flight has its own playful style.

What factors such as energy, accessibility or cost did your team consider?

The site respects reduced motion settings and works with a keyboard and screen readers. Heavy 3D effects load late and pause when not needed, and images are compressed to save data. Every tool is free, and the site can be hosted at no cost.
